summary:
Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021. Penal Code Sections 213 and 214, the 'unnatural sex' provisions carrying one month to one year of imprisonment, were voted down by the lower house 43-1 in June 2019; the upper house reinserted the ban, and a December 2020 joint sitting resolved that homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex. The Penal Code Amendment Act entered into force on 17 February 2021, and no reversal has followed. The provisions had gone unenforced for at least 15 years before repeal.

The repeal did not create a protective framework. Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics. Discrimination and stigma persist, with health-care access singled out as a domain where trans and LGBTIQ people are turned away or poorly served.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. Administrative changes to gender markers on identity documents are suspended because standardised guidelines do not exist, leaving trans people with documents that do not match their presentation.

That document mismatch has direct consequences for reporting crime. Trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault. A 49-year-old trans woman interviewed by Bhutan Broadcasting Service in November 2024 described having nowhere to report violence: police dismiss her cases on the reasoning that her identity card reads male, so 'both parties are men'. Families pressure victims to accept what has happened as fate, and assistance routed through the national LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. The result is practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

LGBTIQ organisations may register and operate legally, including Rainbow Bhutan, though activists describe the registration process as lengthy and burdensome.

Official engagement exists at institutional level. UNFPA Bhutan's 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, the Attorney General's Office and the Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians. Two consultation workshops brought community members together with UN representatives and the National Commission for Women and Children.

Public trans visibility remains exceptional. Dechen, described as one of only two trans women living publicly in Bhutan, fought at 16 to wear the female school uniform kira, a first in Bhutanese society. The LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, started around 2013-2014, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population. LGBTIQ Bhutanese otherwise report near-total social invisibility rather than overt persecution: there is no shared language for gay or trans identities, and lesbianism is under-recognised.
tangentialFactors:
Bhutan's repeal lowered the global tally of states criminalising consensual same-sex conduct from 72 to 71 in March 2021, placing it among a small group of jurisdictions that have legislated out of criminalisation rather than been compelled to by a court.

The legislative path was contested rather than smooth: the upper house moved to restore the ban after the lower house vote, and the final position was settled by a joint sitting clarification rather than a clean amendment. The trajectory since has been stable, with no post-2021 reversal recorded in the sources.

The gap between institutional engagement and street-level outcomes is the defining pattern. Training of justice-sector bodies and first parliamentary dialogue coexist with police refusal to take reports from trans complainants, so formal decriminalisation has not yet translated into enforceable protection.

Social conditions lean toward invisibility rather than confrontation. Reporting describes little persecution or violence in everyday life alongside near-total lack of public recognition, no shared vocabulary for trans and gay identities, and under-recognised lesbianism. Public figures such as Dechen and activists including Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten are exceptions that mark how narrow the space for open visibility remains.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking to formalise an LGBTIQ organisation must pass a registration process that activists characterise as lengthy and burdensome, even though registration is legally permitted.

Trans residents cannot obtain legal gender recognition, and administrative changes to gender markers on identity documents are suspended pending standardised guidelines. Until those guidelines exist, documents will continue to contradict presentation for anyone who has transitioned socially.

Reporting anti-trans violence is obstructed at the first step. Police decline cases where the complainant's identity card records a male sex marker, reasoning that both parties are men. Where a case is accepted and routed through the national LGBTQIA+ committee, response is slow, and families commonly press the victim to accept the assault as fate.

Health-care access is the domain where discrimination and stigma are most consistently reported, and no anti-discrimination statute gives a remedy when a facility refuses service.

Community organising has a documented history: the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, founded by Karma Dupchen in 2013, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population, and the first direct dialogue between LGBTIQ+ community members and parliamentarians took place in 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources give two different start dates for the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, one around 2014 and one in 2013; the discrepancy is unresolved in the inventory.

Whether the suspension of administrative gender-marker changes has a stated review date, or which ministry holds the file, is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory records police guidance, training or disciplinary outcomes addressing the refusal to take reports from trans complainants, so the practical impunity finding rests on victim testimony rather than on documented institutional response.

Whether the 2024 Free & Equal training produced any change in Royal Court of Justice or Attorney General's Office practice is not stated in the sources.

The claim that trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault is reported without a stated methodology or baseline population in the inventory.

Entry, visa and document requirements for visitors are not covered by any source in this inventory.
